title: Where Animals Live
objectives: I can name a habitat and tell what animals live there.
I can tell the difference between a nest, a burrow, and a shelter.
I can tell how an animal is protected.
I can tell how some animals hunt for food.
rationale: Animal homes are an easy way into early animal science. Habitat is the big idea, nest and burrow are two specific homes children can picture, and shelter links to the weather unit. Protect and hunt give two reasons an animal needs a safe place. The unit revisits weather, reason, and storm, because a shelter keeps an animal safe from the weather, and the reason an animal digs or builds is often a storm or a hunter.

passage.title: Two Homes in One Habitat
paras: A little mouse lives in a burrow under a tree. The burrow is its shelter from the storm. Above the tree, an owl sits in a nest. Owls hunt at night, so the mouse stays inside. The burrow protects it. This habitat has a home for both animals.

qs.q: The burrow protects the mouse. What does protects mean?
qs.why: The burrow keeps the mouse safe from the owl and the storm.

teacher.overview: Children learn six words about where animals live and what they do there, then use them to describe one animal's home. The unit revisits weather, reason, and storm.

notes.va.habitat.n: Habitat is the whole place: pond, forest, desert. Show pictures and ask 'Who lives here?' Nest and burrow are parts of a habitat, not the same thing.
notes.va.nest.n: Use a real or picture nest and ask what it is made of. Not every animal builds a nest; contrast with burrow.
notes.va.burrow.n: Draw a side view of a hole in the ground. Children often call any animal home a nest, so sort animal homes into nest and burrow.
notes.va.shelter.n: Shelter keeps animals safe from weather and from other animals. Tie it to the storm word from the weather unit.
notes.va.protect.v: Protect means keep safe from harm. Act it out: one child is the baby bird and another protects it. Have children name one way an animal protects itself.
notes.va.hunt.v: Hunt is about catching animals for food. Keep it simple and true, such as owls and mice or lions in a group. Avoid describing hunting as cruel or kind.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'This picture shows a pond. A pond is a habitat. A bird has a nest in the reeds, and a frog hides under a leaf for shelter. The nest protects the eggs. At night, an owl may hunt near the pond, so the frog stays hidden. I can say where each animal lives.'
discuss: What animals live in a habitat near your home?
Why do animals need a shelter in a storm?
misconceptions: Every animal lives in a nest.
A burrow is the same as a nest.
A habitat is only a house.
extend: Children build a habitat from a shoebox and tell who lives there.
Sort pictures of animals by where they live: nest, burrow, or other shelter.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit nest and burrow the next day with a sorting game, again at one week, and use habitat and protect when you read animal books. Habitat returns when children describe doers in unit 10.

wida.oral: Partner A says where an animal lives and what it does without saying the animal's name. Partner B guesses the animal and names its home.

needsReview: Spanish glosses (hábitat, nido, madriguera, refugio, proteger, cazar) are not reviewed by a native speaker; madriguera and refugio have close alternatives (guarida, albergue).
Fact claims in passages and examples (owls hunt mice at night, moles dig burrows, wolves hunt in groups, polar bears live in the Arctic) are standard facts but should get a quick science check.
